ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Sports Medicine Referral — Rocky Marciano — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: Establishing primary care after retirement from professional boxing: low back pain and left leg pain after a recent disc herniation, left thumb pain, weight gain and blood pressure after stopping training, a brain health baseline, mood, anxiety and sleep, and a sports medicine consultation

text.paragraph: A 32-year-old retired professional heavyweight boxer, four months out of training, with a left L4-L5 disc herniation and L5 radiculopathy a few weeks old on a background of years of low back pain, post-traumatic osteoarthritis of the left thumb base, weight gain after stopping training, and a career of repetitive head impacts. Please advise on the back and leg, the thumb, a brain health baseline and an exercise plan for retirement. [S]

list.item: Does the disc herniation need repeat imaging or a surgical opinion now, and what would change that?
What exercise therapy do you advise for the radiculopathy and the chronic back pain, and when can he run and train again?
How should the post-traumatic osteoarthritis of the left thumb base be treated, and is an injection needed?
What should a brain health baseline after his career include, is brain imaging indicated, and how often should it be repeated?
What exercise and weight plan do you advise now that heavy training has stopped, and what should he avoid?

text.paragraph: Low back pain for about seven years of training and fighting. A few weeks ago, bending to lift a child, he had sharp back pain into the left buttock and calf; an emergency department MRI showed a left paracentral L4-L5 disc extrusion contacting the left L5 root. Leg pain is now intermittent, with slight numbness over the top of the left foot; no weakness, saddle numbness or bladder or bowel change. Oswestry 36%, back pain 6 out of 10. Left thumb base pain on pinch and grip; X-ray today shows first carpometacarpal narrowing and an old healed fracture at the base of the first metacarpal. About thirteen years of boxing with heavy sparring; no remembered loss of consciousness; no cognitive, mood or behavioral complaints; MoCA 29, PHQ-9 3, GAD-7 4, PROMIS sleep T-score 55. Weight 92.0 kg (BMI 28.7), up about 9 kg since he stopped training; blood pressure 136/86 mmHg, home readings started; LDL 137 mg/dL, HbA1c 5.4%, creatinine 1.08 mg/dL. Started today: naproxen 500 mg twice a day with food for two weeks, then as needed, and diclofenac gel on the thumb. No other medicines; no known allergy; never smoked [S]

list.item: Back and leg pain since bending to lift a child, and an old back ache, which stop him driving far or training. [S]
An aching left thumb when he grips or opens a jar. [S]
He has put on weight since he stopped training and wants to stay in shape and healthy for his family. [S]
He has read about boxers whose memory and speech fail later in life and wants to know his own state now. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Rocco Francis Marchegiano was born on September 1, 1923, in Brockton, Massachusetts, where his father, Pierino, worked in a shoe factory; he later boxed as Rocky Marciano. [D]
As a small child he had pneumonia and was not expected to survive. [D]
He was drafted into the Army in 1943, served in Britain, and completed his service in March 1946 at Fort Lewis, Washington; he took up boxing in the Army. [D]
He turned professional in March 1947 and won the world heavyweight championship on September 23, 1952, in Philadelphia, knocking out Jersey Joe Walcott in the thirteenth round. [D]
Broken hands, back injuries and many facial cuts were among the injuries he had during his career. [D]

By one account he knew from August 1949 that he was fighting with a ruptured disc in his back, and from 1951 he had an arthritic right elbow that left his right arm slightly shorter than the left. [D]
He was unbeaten as a professional, retiring with 49 wins in 49 bouts, 43 by knockout; he is the only heavyweight champion to retire with a perfect record. [D]
He trained exceptionally hard: more than once he sparred about 250 rounds to prepare for a fight, about 100 more than usual, and he limited his diet. [D]

On April 27, 1956, at 32, he announced his retirement as undefeated heavyweight champion, saying he wanted to spend more time with his family. Accounts also mention that he was weary of training, at odds with his manager over money, did not want to fight past his prime, and had an ailing back. [D]
In July 1956, after he felt pain in his back while playing with his three-year-old daughter, he checked into a hospital and was diagnosed with a ruptured disc in his back. [D]
He married in 1950; he and his wife had a daughter and later adopted a son. [D]

list.item: Chronic mechanical low back pain for about seven years of heavy training and fighting, aching across the lower back, worse after long drives and in the morning: active, confirmed [S]

Lumbar disc herniation at L4-L5 with left L5 radiculopathy, a few weeks old and improving: sharp pain into the left buttock and calf after bending to lift a child at home, seen in a hospital emergency department, where MRI showed a left paracentral L4-L5 disc extrusion contacting the left L5 nerve root; leg pain now intermittent, with slight numbness over the top of the left foot and normal strength; no bladder or bowel change: active, confirmed [S]

Post-traumatic osteoarthritis of the left thumb base (first carpometacarpal joint) after an old fracture at the base of the first metacarpal from his early fighting years, with pain on pinching and gripping, an ache after long gripping, and a positive grind test: active, confirmed [S]
Overweight after retirement, with a weight gain of about 9 kg in the four months since he stopped training, eating as he did in training camp; BMI 28.7: active, confirmed [S]
Elevated blood pressure reading at intake (136/86 mmHg, average of two) without a diagnosis of hypertension; home readings to confirm: active, confirmed [S]

History of repetitive head impacts from about thirteen years of Army, amateur and professional boxing, including heavy sparring; no remembered loss of consciousness; normal brain health baseline (no cognitive, mood or behavioral complaints; MoCA 29); traumatic encephalopathy syndrome not suspected: active, confirmed [S]

Back and leg pain: neurological examination of the legs at every visit; red flags reviewed (new weakness, saddle numbness, bladder or bowel change, fever, weight loss) with instructions to come the same day if any appear; the outside MRI reviewed and no repeat imaging unless the deficit progresses; naproxen with food for two weeks then as needed; heat and staying active; no opioids, no muscle relaxants, no bed rest. Guideline: Noninvasive Treatments for Acute, Subacute, and Chronic Low Back Pain: A Clinical Practice Guideline From the American College of Physicians (2017) [S]

Thumb base: X-ray of the hand; topical diclofenac gel; hand-protection advice. Guideline: 2019 American College of Rheumatology/Arthritis Foundation Guideline for the Management of Osteoarthritis of the Hand, Hip, and Knee (2019); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, rheumatoid arthritis/osteoarthritis, hypertension and hyperlipidemia monographs (2026) [S]

Weight and cardiovascular risk after heavy training: home blood pressure monitoring with a validated upper-arm cuff, twice a day for a week, before any diagnosis; a meal plan matched to his lower energy needs; lipids and HbA1c at intake; repeat risk assessment yearly. Guideline: 2025 AHA/ACC/AANP/AAPA/ABC/ACCP/ACPM/AGS/AMA/ASPC/NMA/PCNA/SGIM Guideline for the Prevention, Detection, Evaluation and Management of High Blood Pressure in Adults (2025); 2026 ACC/AHA/AACVPR/ABC/ACPM/ADA/AGS/APhA/ASPC/NLA/PCNA Guideline on the Management of Dyslipidemia (2026) [S]

Brain health baseline after repetitive head impacts: symptom inventory (headache, memory, attention, mood, behavior, sleep, balance), MoCA, PHQ-9, GAD-7 and PROMIS sleep at intake; no brain imaging without an indication; repeat yearly; traumatic encephalopathy syndrome is a research diagnosis and is not made on history alone. Guideline: National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke Consensus Diagnostic Criteria for Traumatic Encephalopathy Syndrome (2021) [S]

Mood and anxiety: PHQ-9 and GAD-7 at intake and again at twelve weeks; support for the change of life after retirement. Guideline: Anxiety Disorders in Adults: Screening (2023); Depression and Suicide Risk in Adults: Screening (2023) [S]
Referral to sports medicine, Tobias Achterberg-Lund, MD, ordered 1956-08-04 [S]
